t: LeetCode 1620 — Coordinate With Maximum Network Quality
o: The signal at an integer point (x, y) is the sum over all towers within Euclidean distance radius of floor(q / (1 + d)); farther towers contribute nothing. We must return the integral coordinate with maximal quality, breaking ties toward the lexicographically smallest non-negative point. Example 1 shows the mechanics at (2, 1): the three reachable towers contribute floor(7/(1+0)) + floor(5/(1+√2)) + floor(9/(1+1)) = 7 + 2 + 4 = 13, and no other point does better. Every coordinate and the radius are at most 50, so any point receiving positive signal lies within radius of some tower, confining all interesting points to [0, 100] × [0, 100]. That bounds the search to 101·101 lattice points against ≤ 50 towers — about half a million cheap evaluations — a clear green light for brute force.
k: All coordinates ≤ 50 and radius ≤ 50 confine every relevant point to the box [0, 100] × [0, 100].
Use squared distance for the reachability test; only the quality formula itself needs a square root.
Scanning x ascending then y with a strict '>' update automatically yields the lexicographically smallest optimum — including (0, 0) when everything scores zero.

a.i: Evaluate every lattice point in [0, 100]^2 by summing floor(q / (1 + d)) over towers whose squared distance is at most radius squared. Track the best score with strict improvement so earlier — lexicographically smaller — points win ties, and initialize with a sentinel below zero so (0, 0) wins when all qualities vanish.
s: For x = 0..100, y = 0..100: start with q = 0.
For each tower compute the squared distance; if it is ≤ radius^2 add floor(q_i / (1 + sqrt(d2))).
Update the best only when q strictly exceeds it.
a.t: O(G² · T) with G = 101 grid side and T ≤ 50 towers — roughly 5·10⁵ operations.

a.i: Positive signal can exist only within radius of some tower, so clamp the search grid to the towers' bounding box expanded by radius on each side, intersected with the non-negative quadrant (the answer must be non-negative). The evaluation loop is identical; fewer points are visited. This matters more if constraints were larger, but it also demonstrates geometric reasoning in an interview.
s: Compute min/max of tower x and y coordinates.
Iterate x over [max(0, minX - radius), maxX + radius] and y analogously.
Score each point exactly as in Approach 1 with strict-improvement updates.
a.t: O(W · H · T) where W, H ≤ 2·radius + 1 — same worst case as Approach 1 but typically several times faster.

## Wrap-up

Either version passes comfortably; state the bounding-box argument explicitly since it shows geometric reasoning rather than blind enumeration. **Pitfalls:** drifting outside the non-negative quadrant (the answer must be non-negative — clamp at 0); using < instead of ≤ for reachability (boundary distance still counts); letting tie-breaking depend on floating-point noise — compare only the accumulated integer floors.

**Edge cases:** a single tower answers its own location; all-zero qualities must return [0, 0]; ties resolved lexicographically fall out of the ascending scan order. **Follow-ups:** huge grids — restrict evaluation to lattice points near towers or use gradient ascent from tower peaks; fractional coordinates; or weighted coverage queries answered offline with a sweep.
